item.title: Regulation as a Feature: The Case for AI Transparency
item.description:
Every conversation about the EU AI Act’s transparency rules starts from the same assumption: this is a cost to minimize. Add the disclosure, tick the box, move on. This framing gets the opportunity backwards. AI transparency, done properly, is a genuine competitive advantage for a small AI-using team that competes against operators who treat it as an afterthought.

The obligation, stated plainly

Article 50 of the AI Act requires providers of certain AI systems to state clearly that people interact with AI. It also requires marking of AI-generated or manipulated content, including deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. These duties apply from 2 August 2026. Following the 2026 Digital Omnibus, generative AI systems already on the market before that date get an extended transitional period to 2 December 2026 to comply with the content-marking requirement specifically.

item.title: AI Vendor Lock-In: The Startup Audit You Should Run Before Scale
item.description: The European Parliament’s ITRE committee published a detailed study on European Software and Cyber Dependencies in December 2025. It maps how €264 billion per year flows out of Europe to foreign cloud and software vendors, roughly 1.5% of EU GDP, and why the outflow keeps growing despite a decade of digital sovereignty rhetoric. What stopped me from reading it as a policy document was not the numbers. It was the mechanism. The four vectors of AI vendor lock-in it describes at EU scale, proprietary formats, API dependencies, long contracts, and network effects, are the same ones startups build into their products right now, sprint by sprint.

item.title: AI Adoption Risks Every European SME Should Know About
item.description: Most European SMEs that adopt AI tools right now make the same decision large enterprises made a decade ago with cloud software, and they are about to discover the same consequences. Tool by tool, subscription by subscription, the dependency architecture builds. By the time the regulatory environment catches up, the cost of changing course is already significant. The December 2025 European Parliament study on software and cyber dependencies puts hard numbers on what this looks like at scale. These numbers are worth knowing before your next renewal or sign-up.

item.title: Enterprise AI in Europe: The Hidden Cost of Vendor Lock-In
item.description: The European Parliament’s December 2025 study on software and cyber dependencies puts a number on something most enterprise leaders already sense but have not yet formally mapped. Roughly 80% of EU cloud and software spending flows to US companies. Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud together control approximately 70% of European cloud infrastructure. Microsoft 365 holds around 90% of the enterprise productivity suite market. The three US hyperscalers together hold more European cloud market share than every European provider combined, by a factor of roughly ten to one. This is not a new finding. The study makes one thing visible, and most enterprise risk frameworks have not yet caught up with it: AI adoption is not a separate layer above this concentration. It is the mechanism that accelerates it.

item.title: European Research's AI Problem: Implementation, Not Adoption
item.description:
Understanding where an industry stands on AI adoption is useful. Mapping it systematically, with verified sources, structured synthesis, and clear conclusions, is a different skill. This case study documents a deep research sprint on AI integration across European research institutes. It covers the question, the AI-assisted research method, the evidence, and the strategic meaning.

AI integration in European research institutes is accelerating, at least on paper. Institutes approve strategies. They form committees. They issue press releases. But if you ask most researchers and research managers what AI tools they use in their day-to-day work, and how, the honest answer is usually a shrug, a mention of ChatGPT for emails, and a vague sense that the institution is “working on it.”

item.title: Mapping AI Adoption Across European Research Institutes: A Deep Research Case Study
item.description: Understanding where an industry stands on AI adoption is useful. Mapping it systematically, with verified sources, structured synthesis, and actionable conclusions, is a different skill. This case study documents a deep research sprint on AI integration across European research institutes. It covers the question, how the research team investigated it using AI-assisted research tools, what the evidence shows, and what it means strategically. It is also a worked example of what AI-assisted research analysis looks like in practice, as distinct from AI-generated content.
